description: This week's lecture covers how processes manage their own memory and communicate independently.
When a process terminates due to receiving a signal, it triggers the kernel's awareness and allows the parent process to continue.
Setting up new processes incurs overhead due to context switching; allowing children to terminate directly reduces unnecessary computations.
Processes can execute synchronously without creating new ones; they share resources and data, allowing for efficient communication between them.
This segment explains synchronous (sequential) and asynchronous (parallel) processes in computing, highlighting their differences.
Signals allow asynchronous event handling without modifying existing code. A signal handler sets a flag when an event occurs.

We discuss asynchronous events like keyboard presses moving dynamically without knowing their timing. Pipes enable both synchronous and asynchronous communication, showing how they fit into different scenarios.
Explains how buffers manage data flow between processes, discussing shared memory's benefits and limitations.
We create two file descriptors and model a pipe as a queue. Every write ends up being read in reverse order.
Explains how pipes work with file descriptors, initializing them to -1 as placeholders.
Explains how processes communicate through pipes, moving data segments between them.
Reading data from a pipe involves using file descriptors, buffers, and heap memory to manage large amounts of data efficiently.
Explains how to allocate and initialize memory on the stack, focusing on setting values like null.
After freeing memory and closing file descriptors, additional cleanup steps include framing memory and optimizing code repetition.
Explains encoding as filling data with numbers or ASCII characters to track position within strings.
Child process continues without waiting for data from pipe; data is available instantly.
Shows how pipes allow concurrent execution of parent and child processes, with child waiting on write completion.
In parallel processes sharing resources, closing file descriptors ensures proper resource management.
Child process creates a pipe, waits for input, closes file descriptors, exits with return code. Parent captures child's return code using `wait`.
Explains how buffering works in pipes, comparing it to a single-process scenario and discussing potential issues with large numbers.
Two pipes are needed for bidirectional communication. Each pipe uses two file descriptors and reads from them.
If sending a message from a child process to its parent involves writing to a file descriptor and reading back, demonstrating how processes communicate through shared memory.
Explains how parent writes to child's pipe and child reads from it in a circular synchronous manner.
Process A writes to shared text, synchronizing with child's read of shared text.
Even if pipes are created beforehand, they need a hierarchical structure controlled through forks, leading to complex but often impractical process trees.
We can avoid sending signals between arbitrary processes; instead, we describe their meanings beforehand, making it easier to design systems where processes change over time.
Explains how IPC pipes allow sharing file descriptors across processes without hierarchical dependencies.
File descriptors are integer identifiers for open files or streams. They start after the initial set of file descriptors when creating pipes.
Shows how file descriptors in a process increase sequentially starting at 0.
Explains how using pre-existing file descriptor indices simplifies checking active file descriptors compared to visiting each one individually.
Explains how bit masking can efficiently monitor file descriptors for readable data.
